thumb.title: Last place knocked out the leader

concept: The story is an upset at the very last hurdle, so the hero is built as a setup and a sting: 'Arjun led the group with one game to go' sits in muted grey and 'Vaishali, in last place, beat him' lands in white, with the two point totals (16 and 7) that show how unlikely it was. Slide 2 is the final Group D table as bars, with only the top bar lit, because the whole drama is that just one player goes through and 16 points ended up third on tie-break. Slide 3 walks through the two swings of the day move by move, slide 4 widens out with a big 0 (Indians left in the title semis) and slide 5 sets up what's next and asks fans whether the format is too harsh. Indian-sports orange, type only: no player photos and no event or federation logos.
caption:
Last place beat the group leader. And it cost India its best title shot in Budapest.

Arjun Erigaisi went into the final game of the Total Chess group stage on top of Group D. He had just beaten R Vaishali. Then Vachier-Lagrave won, so Arjun needed a win to finish first. Instead Vaishali, bottom of the group, outplayed him with about a minute on her clock and Arjun resigned on move 61.

Arjun finished on 16 points, level with Hans Niemann but third on tie-break. Only group winners play for the title, so no Indian is left in the four-player title knockout. Praggnanandhaa finished last in Group B and Magnus Carlsen went winless in the group stage.

One loss and you're out of the title race. Too harsh, or exactly why this format is exciting? Tell us below.
